summary:
Grain Storm is a Python FastAPI backend for field-level crop planning from open NASA and FAO data. A farmer's polygon is converted to area, perimeter and coordinates, and everything downstream hangs off that point or grid cell.
Data layer: NASA POWER, ERA5 via Open-Meteo (rainfall, ET0, ERA5-Land soil moisture), GPM IMERG V07 rainfall and SMAP L4 soil moisture. IMERG is pulled as single-cell OPeNDAP slices and SMAP through AppEEARS point tasks, run by a background worker. FAO GAEZ v4 suitability, crop calendars and yields are sampled without downloading global rasters, and SSURGO adds soil context. Everything lands in a SQLite cache keyed by source, version, location and UTC date, with provenance. Missing values stay missing, never zero.
Analysis: a daily water budget using FAO-56 ETc = ET0 × Kc across crop stages, plus nutrient accounting, rotation scheduling and what-if scenarios.
API: POST /v1/rotation-advice runs the full analysis. /v1/context, /v1/crop-suitability, /v1/crop-calendar and /v1/plans expose the individual parts.
AI layer: POST /api/v1/intelligence sends the analysis to Gemini for a structured draft. An independent validator then checks dates, units and evidence before the report is returned.
details:
GrainStorm is a Python backend for geospatial agricultural analysis and crop-rotation decision support. It combines satellite and weather data acquisition, source-backed agricultural reference datasets, deterministic daily simulations, and an optional AI interpretation layer. Its central purpose is to make the relationships between crop order, seasonal timing, soil-water availability, nutrient constraints, and farm economics explicit and traceable.

The project is delivered through a FastAPI HTTP service and command-line tools. Its outputs are structured JSON reports containing calculations, data provenance, missing-input assessments, scenario comparisons, and validation findings. This architecture allows research tools, agricultural applications, or future client interfaces to use the same analytical backend.

Field geometry and analysis orchestration

The primary workflow begins at POST /v1/rotation-advice. A request supplies a GeoJSON farm polygon, crop sequence, preferred planting date, planning horizon, and optional soil, irrigation, management, weather, and economic inputs.

The geometry module validates the polygon’s coordinate structure, closure, distinct vertices, and nondegenerate area. It calculates approximate area, perimeter, and centroid using a local equirectangular projection and polygon geometry. The centroid selects location-dependent environmental datasets, while polygon-derived hectares scale per-hectare quantities into whole-field water volumes, nutrient totals, production benchmarks, and financial estimates.

The system explicitly distinguishes spatial support: sampling a coarse dataset at a farm’s centroid does not turn that dataset into a field measurement.

The rotation orchestrator assembles crop suitability, calendars, historical yield baselines, soil context, and weather inputs before constructing simulation scenarios. For a sequence of distinct crops, it can enumerate every crop-order permutation and compare their consequences under the supplied assumptions.

Environmental and agricultural data integration

GrainStorm implements adapters for several complementary sources:

  • NASA GPM IMERG Final V07 precipitation, including bounded single-cell OPeNDAP acquisition and daily normalization.
  • NASA SMAP soil-moisture sampling through AppEEARS, preserving product metadata and observation counts.
  • ERA5 weather through Open-Meteo, including precipitation and reference evapotranspiration.
  • NASA POWER temperature, precipitation, and relative humidity.
  • FAO/IIASA GAEZ v4 location-based crop suitability, historical crop-cycle anchors and durations, and historical yield baselines.
  • USDA SSURGO soil properties for covered United States locations.
  • USDA NASS agricultural yield and price records, with explicit record selection and unit conversion.

Seven crop profiles are supported: grain maize, grain soybean, wheat, sorghum, chickpea, sunflower, and wetland rice.

Source adapters retain information such as requested coordinates, dataset identity, reference period, units, spatial resolution, and coverage limitations. Historical yield and suitability layers are presented as regional baselines rather than future yield forecasts or crop-success probabilities.

Daily water-balance simulation

The deterministic planner models crop sequences over daily weather records, carrying soil-water conditions through crop periods and intervening gaps. It accounts for rainfall, evapotranspiration demand, available storage, irrigation, and unmet water demand under the configured model.

The standard pathway uses crop-stage coefficients with reference evapotranspiration:

ETc = Kc × ET0

An optional FAO-56-inspired dual-coefficient pathway separates basal crop transpiration from soil evaporation and applies a root-zone water-stress coefficient:

ETc,actual = (Kcb × Ks + Ke) × ET0

The implementation calculates stage-dependent basal coefficients, root-zone depletion, readily available water, soil evaporation reduction, and the exposed wetted fraction. These calculations make the water-demand estimate responsive to supplied soil and crop parameters rather than assigning one fixed water requirement to an entire season.

Irrigation inputs can include application efficiency, seasonal limits, costs, and farmer decisions to accept, skip, or replace an automatic recommendation. The report preserves both the recommendation and the applied decision.

Water depth is converted into field volume using the relationship:

1 mm over 1 hectare = 10 m³

The backend also supports management zones with area fractions and independent soil, management, or irrigation overrides. Zone calculations are aggregated into field-level results while retaining the underlying zone context.

Crop scheduling and sequence feasibility

The planner supports recurring planting windows, including windows that cross calendar years, crop-specific durations, turnaround gaps, and planning-horizon checks. It can evaluate fixed scheduling or move a crop to its next permitted planting window.

Reports expose planting dates, harvest dates, configured gaps, seasonal waiting periods, and feasibility issues. This makes the cost of a particular crop order visible: a sequence may require additional seasonal waiting even when each crop is individually suitable.

Regional GAEZ dates remain provisional calendar anchors. They are not treated as locally validated planting instructions.

Nutrient budgets and conditional economics

GrainStorm supports explicit nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium accounting. Where sufficient inputs are supplied, nutrient removal can be derived from expected yield and sourced removal coefficients:

Nutrient removal, kg/ha = yield, t/ha × removal coefficient, kg/t

Budgets can incorporate fertilizer application and recovery, residue release, other losses, and biological nitrogen fixation. Fixation is reported separately so its interpretation remains visible.

The economics pathway supports yield, marketable production, crop selling prices, itemized production costs, additional income, and irrigation costs. Outputs can include gross revenue, total cost, net margin, return on cost, and break-even indicators. Missing local prices or costs remain missing rather than being silently converted into zero.

An optional multi-criteria ranking mechanism normalizes available scenario metrics and applies caller-selected weights. Criteria include margin, irrigation, unmet water demand, nutrient shortfalls, and pest/disease rotation scores. Scenarios lacking required metrics or established calendar feasibility are excluded with reasons. The resulting score is a transparent comparison under selected priorities.

Input resolution and uncertainty

The input resolver gives caller-provided values precedence. When automatic resolution is enabled, it can fill selected gaps with documented reference values or planning assumptions and return their sources, confidence labels, and replacement guidance. Strict mode instead requires the missing inputs.

The integrated API exposes four analysis states: processing, needs_input, preliminary, and complete. These distinguish unfinished acquisition from missing information and calculated reports.

Future weather is handled separately from historical observations. Operational forecasts are bounded to the supported short horizon; longer periods require explicitly supplied weather scenarios with complete date coverage.

Evidence-aware AI interpretation

The optional POST /api/v1/intelligence endpoint accepts a completed or preliminary analysis and builds a compact evidence context for Google Gemini using the official google-genai SDK.

Gemini generates a Pydantic-constrained AIDecisionDraft. Python independently checks supported crop identifiers, evidence references, structured numerical claims and units, proposed dates, durations, planning horizons, sequence consistency, and relevant water or feasibility constraints.

Python assigns proposal-validation outcomes and report metadata. The model cannot grant itself backend validation.

The resulting versioned report includes an executive decision, crop recommendations, planting and harvest proposals, resource findings, risks, prioritised actions, sequence comparisons, planning guidance, and an audit trail. Evidence-reference checks and numerical consistency checks improve accountability, while free-text agronomic claims still require expert review.

Reliability and implementation

The stack includes Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, Pandas, Requests, SQLite, NetCDF4, Earthaccess, Matplotlib, and Google GenAI.

Satellite acquisition uses persistent jobs, bounded downloads, overlapping-request deduplication, transactional job claiming, and retained NASA task identifiers for restart recovery. SQLite also supports environmental caching and AI draft caching.

AI generation has configurable concurrency, timeout, input-size, output-size, retry, and per-analysis call limits. Stable cache keys incorporate normalized context, model configuration, prompt version, and schema version.

Automated tests cover API contracts, calculations, geometry, weather coverage, source normalization, job handling, and AI validation. AI tests use mocked provider responses. Repository documentation additionally records bounded live IMERG and SMAP acquisition checks; these establish acquisition functionality rather than agricultural accuracy.

Originality and intended impact

GrainStorm’s contribution is the integration of geospatial data engineering, explicit agricultural calculations, and independently checked AI interpretation into one inspectable backend workflow. Users can examine how a result was calculated, which evidence supports it, and what information is still missing.

The intended impact is better-informed comparison of crop sequences and earlier identification of water, nutrient, timing, and input constraints. Quantified improvements in yield, water savings, profitability, or sustainability have not yet been established. Field evaluation, agronomist review, regional calibration, and production deployment hardening remain the next steps toward demonstrating those outcomes.
